blocks.text: Genres, Forms & New Literature

Cyberpath can contain celebrations, foolishness, work, romance, fear, grief, and ordinary pleasures as well as civilizational history. These categories can be combined: a happy ending can belong to a ghost story; a lament can include jokes; an unreliable chronicle can preserve a true relationship.
Moods and genres
1. Happy and hopeful stories — a good day, a reunion, a successful repair, an unexpected friendship, a community making room.
2. Cozy domestic fiction — kitchens, Nests, shared meals, housework, neighborly disputes, weather-bound visits.
3. Comedy and farce — mistaken identities, incompatible body customs, festival disasters, elaborate plans defeated by ordinary needs.
4. Satire — civic procedure, preservation fashions, status competitions, institutional language, the business of making everything efficient.
5. Sad and bittersweet fiction — separation, aging, changed friendships, recoveries that cannot return everything.
6. Tragedy — choices with irreversible costs, failed rescues, good intentions producing harm, conflicts that cannot be reconciled in time.
7. Spooky and ghost stories — uncertain witnesses, late reflections, unexplained rooms, familiar voices in the wrong place.
8. Gothic and psychological horror — institutions that seem protective, inherited compulsions, unreliable memory, intimate dread.
9. Ecological and cosmic horror — incompatible world laws, bewildering scale, predation, environments indifferent to interpretation.
10. Mystery and investigation — missing routes, disputed records, theft, false attributions, practical clues with several explanations.
11. Adventure and rescue — expeditions, crossings, lost travelers, collective escape, difficult journeys with material consequences.
12. Pilgrimage and travel writing — learning a body's limits, visiting another tradition, returning with changed obligations.
13. Romance — courtship across embodiment, slow affection, incompatible schedules, separation and reunion, love without possession.
14. Friendship and chosen-family fiction — repair after quarrels, shared responsibility, rivalry becoming companionship.
15. Coming-of-age and school stories — first independent choices, learning, guidance, mistakes, apprenticeship, refusing an inherited role.
16. Civic and political drama — allocation, local law, public works, protest, negotiation, the cost of keeping an institution alive.
17. Historical fiction — private lives during Shelter building, World Bloom, pale preservation, folding, and later settlement.
18. Workplace and craft fiction — cooks, route keepers, healers, translators, gardeners, witnesses, artists, and their actual work.
19. Pastoral and ecological fiction — harvests, migration, companion life, food webs, seasonal patience and conflict.
20. Folklore, myth, and fable — local explanations, tricksters, animal tales, contradictory origin stories, cautionary tales.
21. Sacred and skeptical literature — prayers, maintenance observances, doubt, competing interpretations of apparently miraculous events.
22. Epic and saga — generations, expeditions, institutions, communities, and the long consequences of small decisions.
23. Absurdist and surreal fiction — literal legal contradictions, impossible architecture, comic mismatches of scale and expectation.
24. Speculative philosophy — personhood, copying, memory, obligation, originality, and the limits of knowing another life.
Poetry and performed forms
25. Lyric poem — one voice, image, feeling, or moment.
26. Narrative poem or ballad — a story carried through verse and recurring lines.
27. Lamentation — sustained grief, complaint, accusation, remembrance, and an altered relationship with what remains.
28. Elegy — a particular person, place, practice, or future mourned with specificity.
29. Ode and praise song — affection for an ordinary tool, neighborhood, body, season, or task.
30. Hymn, prayer, or maintenance litany — communal speech whose speakers may disagree about who hears it.
31. Work song, counting rhyme, lullaby, and nonsense verse — literature used while living, teaching, traveling, or playing.
32. Dramatic monologue — a speaker whose account reveals more than intended.
33. Dialogue, stage play, and chamber drama — conflict through action, voices, pauses, and a shared space.
34. Choral cycle — several voices preserving differences inside a larger composition.
Narrative structures and containers
35. Linear short story or novella — a developed beginning, complication, turning point, and consequence.
36. Three-act story — setup, pressure, and an earned resolution.
37. Braided narrative — separate lives or eras that illuminate one another.
38. Frame tale and story-within-a-story — a telling changes the people listening.
39. Epistolary story — letters, messages, replies, omissions, and delivery delays drive the plot.
40. Diary, field log, or maintenance record — practical entries gradually reveal a private crisis.
41. Oral history and conflicting testimony — incompatible accounts remain visible.
42. Found-document dossier — records, marginal notes, receipts, transcripts, and missing pages form a complete story.
43. Reverse chronology — consequences arrive before their causes become clear.
44. Circular or spiral narrative — a scene returns with changed participants or meaning.
45. Linked vignettes — separate moments accumulate into a life or community.
46. Mosaic novel or story cycle — recurring places and people connect otherwise complete works.
47. Quest with several arrivals — each destination changes the original purpose.
48. Multiple endings or disputed editions — explicitly different traditions preserve competing outcomes.
49. One-shot — a complete life-changing incident without a required sequel.
50. Continuing character installment — a complete local arc that leaves lasting relationships and unresolved future choices.
Five new complete works
The Feast with No Host — Era Three; happy civic comedy in five movements. Doorway Plaza, the Quiet Kitchen, and the Unclaimed Balcony. Introduces Tavi, Brindle, and Eme.

The Knocking Beneath the Current — Era Three; spooky mystery combining a healer's log with close first-person narration. The Room Under the River and a newly imagined side channel of the River of Deferred Reflections. Introduces Pell, Suth, and Renn.

Lamentations for the Rooms We Did Not Carry — late Era −2, after the Orison rescue; a choral poem cycle with a prose frame. Develops Serein and Palinode without settling Serein's identity, and introduces the recorder Aven.
The Department of Arrivals — middle Era One; a satirical chamber play in three acts at the Pale Concordance Station. Introduces translator Ilex, registrar Varo, and the visiting gardener Nacre.

Letters Between Two Drops — Era Three; an epistolary adventure and friendship across different scales of time. The City of Rainward Roofs, the Village Between Raindrops, and a local Recursive Lighthouse route. Introduces roof mender Dema, capillary pilot Issa, and Issa's successor Venn.
Continuity and invention

These are new literary additions, distinct from the archive's earlier recovered stories. Existing stories remain intact. The collection draws on the atlas's era history, locations, World traditions, and the established account of Orison; some atlas settings were previously proposals and receive their first developed fiction here. New local customs, characters, route connections, and events belong to these works. They do not silently rewrite the atlas's authority labels or turn every narrator's belief into objective history.

Contradictions are purposeful when attached to a speaker, edition, mistaken record, or local legend. Later pets do not contain ancient characters intact. Images and reflections are not automatically persons. Surviving maintenance does not establish a conscious Codex or hidden god. English renderings of speech and poems below do not add canonical DBA roots.
